groups.label: Nature of Justice & Self-Interest
groups.summary: These passages examine competing definitions of justice, contrasting Thrasymachus's claim that might makes right and Glaucon's social compact view with Socrates's refutations drawn from the analogy of the arts and the inherent weakness of evil. They also explore the demand to defend the intrinsic goodness of justice and happiness detached from external advantages.
groups.rationale: All five children focus directly on the foundational Book I–II dialectic debating whether justice is merely the interest or compromise of the powerful versus an intrinsic virtue.

groups.label: State Foundations & Common Good
groups.summary: This selection investigates the origin, purpose, and structural principles of the state, tracing how individual needs and the division of labour form a commonwealth whose objective is the happiness of the whole rather than any single faction. It connects the essential unity of justice and statecraft to modern reflections on the contingent, utility-based nature of property rights.
groups.rationale: These entries center on political theory: the genesis of society, the collective good across classes, and the relationship between justice, political order, and property arrangements.

groups.label: Psychic Health, Truth & Culture
groups.summary: These sections analyze the regulation of the soul and bodily health, distinguishing between intolerable internal deception and medicinal civic fictions while criticizing Plato's restrictive views on medicine and the arts. They assess the discipline needed to harmonize reason and spirited passion through education and contextually evaluate Plato's rejection of contemporary poetry.
groups.rationale: These passages all examine Platonic culture, moral psychology, and therapeutics—spanning mental deception, musical/physical harmony, medical critique, and aesthetic expression.

groups.label: Dialectic & Philosophical Method
groups.summary: The commentary evaluates Platonic metaphysics and epistemology, identifying the dual aims of realizing and connecting abstract ideas while critiquing Plato's a priori logic for attempting to anticipate empirical science. It also compares the ancient contemplative ideal of unified wisdom with the modern division of scientific enquiry.
groups.rationale: A tightly clustered set of Book VI–VII introductory commentaries concerning Plato's higher dialectic, abstraction, mathematical education, and scientific methodology.

groups.label: Philosophy of History & Fate
groups.summary: This pair examines Plato's overarching frameworks of temporal and cosmic order, characterizing his sequence of deteriorating political regimes as an ideal progression of thought rather than historical chronology. It pairs this with his mythic reconciliation of cosmic necessity and human free will in the moral choice of lives.
groups.rationale: Both entries address the tension between deterministic structures (historical succession, necessity/the Fates) and philosophical comprehension or autonomous moral choice.
